subject: Help with octopus abundance study design

messages.author: d5e9e2ae8e479201
messages.subject: Help with octopus abundance study design
parts:
Hello unmarked community, 

I am trying to optimize occupancy/binomial mixture modeling for octopuses in California but I am encountering some issues that are likely causing me to violate some assumptions. 

What I have done before: Working within a kelp forest/rocky reef, I surveyed 24 100-m2 transects 3 times within a season and counted all octopuses in two different years. Each transect was at minimum 30 m apart from each other. My later work suggests that octopuses can move much further than this over the course a few days (which I didn't know at the time) and so these surveys likely do not meet the closure assumption. I have been trying to estimate abundances using pcount but my lambda and p values won't converge (I posted this in a previous thread, and I can send my PhD dissertation to anyone who wants more detail). I am now designing a new project to occur in La Jolla, CA and I don't want to repeat the same mistakes as I did before. 

Major Question: 
Any advice on how to define "site" in a mostly continuous and very large ecosystem like a kelp forest/rocky reef? As a SCUBA diver, I am extremely limited in the space I can survey. There are no clear breaks in the habitat, and there is evidence that octopuses can move across apparent breaks anyway. I would like to estimate abundance and not just occupancy, but I am not sure if this is possible given the restrictions of the ecosystem. My thought is to setup a grid of permanent transects across the whole reef, at set them at 500 m apart. Additionally, I am not sure if I can have transect search areas any larger than 100 m2, and my concern is that this is too small of an area to capture any patterns in octopus abundance in relation to habitat characteristics. 

I greatly appreciate any advice. As a prime example of camouflage and crypticuty, I think octopuses are an ideal candidate for this type of modeling, but I definitely have a ways to go to adapt the model to their ecosystem and behavior. Thank you!

Jenny

messages.author: 00ebeb6e0521112d
messages.subject: RE: [unmarked] Help with octopus abundance study design
parts:
Dear Jenny,

First, I think a basic thing to consider would be whether you could individually identify those octopuses ? If yes, then you could do spatial capture-recapture (SCR), which, in a way, would make obsolete some (even if not all) worries about how to define a sample site. One cost though is that the models become more complex.

Second, A "reduced" version, in a sense, of SCR is distance sampling (DS). It seems to me that this might be quite adequate for scuba diving, where a transect could perhaps be defined reasonably easy ? Again, DS relieves you somewhat of the worries of having to define a sample site. Have you considered DS ?

Third, if you want to discretize space and define sample sites, then you're at your current question. I think that this is hard to reply in general. How large a site should be depends on the grain and the range of the environmental variation for which you want to detect variation in density/abundance. Also, there is a relation with the temporal and spatial scale of movements of these octopuses: if they move a lot, then you may want to have bigger sites and shorter intervals between repeated samples.

I wouldn't be afraid of (small) sites that can only contain 1 ind. If you have only 0 and 1 counts and use occupancy, you can still interpret this as abundance, because at small spatial scales the two coincide.

As always, one might be tempted to say "Simulation is the answer": can you imagine ways in which you can simulate your system in order to refine/create some intuition about the best sample design ?

Best regards  --- Marc

messages.author: 527d9b3ec7deff2d
messages.subject: Re: Help with octopus abundance study design
parts:
Hi Jenny,

To expand on Marc's comment, there is a good paper that explains how the design and interpretation of an occupancy model in continuous habitat can be tricky, and depends largely on the density and movement of your focal species: http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1890/ES11-00308.1/abstract

I agree that this system seems more suited to distance sampling, since then you won't have to define a "site" arbitrarily.  The tradeoff is that you want transects long enough to detect your organism, but also enough transects to estimate variation due to habitat features (given your objectives).  There is also the requirement that you can adequately measure the distance to each individual, or at least close enough to be able to assign a distance bin for a multinomial specification (see the distsamp or gdistsamp functions).

messages.author: 1812cd2b1d8ede7e
messages.subject: Re: Help with octopus abundance study design
parts:
Hi Jenny,

Adding on to the comments below  (Marc and Dan are certainly authorities on these models), it might help to better specify your questions/hypotheses.  As a naturalist I'm always tempted to ask general/descriptive questions, but more specific questions would help address the scale of inference and therefore how much the spatial scale matters.  For instance, are you interested in microhabitat use, or whether octopuses are more abundant in a marine sanctuary vs a heavily fished area (ie a much bigger spatial scale)?  Answering those questions for yourself might help you narrow down which models will best answer your question.

Best,
Alex

messages.author: d5e9e2ae8e479201
messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] Help with octopus abundance study design
parts:
Hello Marc, Dan, and Alex, 

Thank you for your informative responses. To answer your questions, I am unable to identify specific individuals, so that rules out SCR. I had considered DS in the past but had ruled it out for reasons I can no longer remember. I will re-visit it now. Thank you! 

I am interested mostly in microhabitat use, and specifically how the interactive effects of shelter quality/availability and predator abundance could be shaping microhabitat use. These surveys are being completed in conjunction with a passive acoustic telemetry study, and under the larger umbrella of abalone restoration (octopuses are major predators on abalone, and we are having trouble predicting and preventing such predation). The issue of scale is one I have struggled with (I would love to study all scales!) because ultimately I want to understand what pieces of information an octopus utilizes to make decisions about movement and habitat use. One of the challenges is that octopuses are notoriously variable and behaviorally plastic, so there are many layers I am trying to keep organized. I appreciate any and all feedback or suggestions! 

Cheers, 
Jenny
